description: We are SAMIR, a multidisciplinary team of passionate young innovators participating in the NASA Space Apps Challenge in Douala, Cameroon. Our interests include software engineering, artificial intelligence, data science, and satellite technologies. We aim to develop an innovative web application that harmonizes MODIS and VIIRS active fire data to help identify historical patterns, monitor unusual fire activity, and support early warning and disaster response.
summary: FIREWATCH AI is a multi-satellite fire intelligence platform developed by Team SAMIR to address NASA's challenge of harmonizing MODIS and VIIRS active fire hotspot observations. The project processes observations from five satellite platforms, preserving their original metadata while exploring how detections from different sensors may relate to the same burning activity. It introduces transparent spatial-temporal association methods to help users examine potential overlapping observations, compare raw detections with candidate associations, and understand uncertainty. Starting with Cameroon, FIREWATCH AI aims to support historical fire analysis, monitoring, and informed disaster-response planning through accessible geospatial data and interactive visualization.
details:
FIREWATCH AI is an AI-assisted, multi-satellite fire intelligence project designed to address the challenge of harmonizing MODIS and VIIRS active fire hotspot observations.

HOW IT WORKS

The platform begins by collecting and processing NASA FIRMS datasets from five satellite sources: MODIS Terra/Aqua, VIIRS Suomi-NPP, NOAA-20 and NOAA-21. Our data pipeline validates the original CSV files, checks their structure and quality, standardizes observation fields, and preserves the original satellite metadata, processing versions and source information.

We have processed 1,130,027 observations from 12 datasets covering 2025 and 2026. The normalized observations are stored in Parquet format for reproducible analysis.

Our central innovation is a transparent spatial-temporal association methodology. It examines observations from different satellites using geographic distance and acquisition-time differences to identify potential cross-satellite relationships. Rather than treating these associations as confirmed fires, the system preserves uncertainty and allows users to distinguish original satellite observations from inferred relationships.

SCIENTIFIC APPROACH

We conducted data-quality assessments, geographical coverage analysis focused on Cameroon, multi-period association experiments and randomized null comparisons. These experiments help us understand how many apparent associations could occur by chance. We also examined satellite pixel dimensions and independent satellite coverage resources to identify opportunities for stronger validation.

BENEFITS AND INTENDED IMPACT

FIREWATCH AI aims to make multi-satellite fire observations easier to explore and interpret. It can support historical burning-activity analysis, identification of unusual observation patterns, and research that informs environmental monitoring and disaster-response planning. Cameroon is our initial demonstration area, while the architecture is designed to support other geographical regions.

TECHNOLOGY AND CREATIVITY

The project uses Python-based data processing, Jupyter notebooks, CSV and Parquet datasets, geospatial analysis and statistical methods. Its creative contribution is not simply displaying hotspot locations, but investigating how observations from different satellite instruments relate to one another while making the assumptions, limitations and uncertainty visible.

We recognize that an active-fire hotspot represents a satellite observation of thermal activity, not necessarily a confirmed wildfire. Our approach therefore prioritizes scientific transparency, reproducibility and responsible interpretation.
